rows.source_label: Equation (1.1): q_t + A q_x = 0 for a constant real m by m matrix A

rows.source_label: The real scalar constant-coefficient equation is hyperbolic
rows.next_foundation: Define hyperbolicity through a real eigenbasis and prove its one-dimensional specialization.

rows.source_label: Equation (1.2): q_t + ubar q_x = 0 for constant advection speed ubar
rows.next_foundation: Specialize the constant-coefficient residual to scalar advection.

rows.source_label: Equation (1.3): q(x,t) = qtilde(x - ubar t) solves the advection equation and propagates unchanged
Equation (1.4): w_t + c w_x = 0 with c positive models a right-going one-way wave

rows.source_label: Equations (1.2) and (1.4) are mathematically identical after renaming the unknown and speed

rows.source_label: Equation (1.5): p_t + K u_x = 0 and u_t + (1/rho) p_x = 0
rows.next_foundation: Audit the two classical acoustic constraints as a definition with explicit derivative and material conventions; rejected certificate projections do not dispose of definition coverage.

rows.source_label: Equation (1.6): q = (p,u) and A = [[0,K],[1/rho,0]]
rows.next_foundation: Define the two-by-two acoustics matrix and prove componentwise equivalence with (1.5).

rows.source_label: For c = sqrt(K/rho), w1 = p + rho c u satisfies w1_t + c w1_x = 0
rows.next_foundation: Prove the right characteristic identity with explicit positivity and square-root hypotheses.

rows.source_label: w2 = p - rho c u satisfies w2_t - c w2_x = 0 and the printed left-going profile is q2(x,t) = qtilde(x+ct)
rows.next_foundation: Prove the left characteristic identity and formally adjudicate the printed q2 versus w2 notation mismatch.

rows.source_label: The two-equation acoustics system decomposes into two scalar waves moving in opposite directions
rows.next_foundation: Package the two characteristic maps as an invertible decomposition.

rows.source_label: A constant-coefficient system is hyperbolic when A has real eigenvalues and m linearly independent eigenvectors
Every vector in R^m decomposes uniquely as a linear combination of the eigenvectors
rows.next_foundation: Reuse the basis representation theorem for the hyperbolic eigenbasis.

rows.source_label: The eigenvalues of A give the speeds of the component waves
rows.next_foundation: Define eigenmode translated profiles and prove their speed-indexed residual identity.

rows.source_label: The acoustics matrix in (1.6) has eigenvalues -c and +c
rows.next_foundation: Exhibit and verify the two acoustics eigenpairs under K = rho c squared.

rows.source_label: Equation (1.7): differentiating (1.5) and eliminating mixed derivatives gives p_tt = c^2 p_xx
rows.next_foundation: Formalize second partial derivatives and the mixed-derivative elimination with explicit regularity.

rows.source_label: Equation (1.8): q_t + f(q)_x = 0 with flux function f
rows.next_foundation: Audit the existing scalar/system flux-divergence solution definition against (1.8), preserving the flux composition and implicit classical regularity.

rows.source_label: Equation (1.9): q_t + f'(q) q_x = 0 is the quasilinear form
rows.next_foundation: Prove the spatial chain-rule equivalence under differentiability of q and f.

rows.source_label: The quasilinear form suggests hyperbolicity when the flux Jacobian satisfies the matrix condition
rows.reason: The passage says only that the quasilinear form suggests a hyperbolicity criterion; it does not assert a theorem or specify hypotheses under which the suggestion is sufficient or necessary.

rows.source_label: Equation (1.1) is a conservation law with linear flux f(q) = A q
rows.next_foundation: Prove the derivative of the linear flux and residual equality.

rows.source_label: Equation (1.10): for any two points x1 and x2, the time derivative of the interval integral is f(q(x1,t)) minus f(q(x2,t))
rows.next_foundation: Audit integral balance for arbitrary two endpoints, with incoming-minus-outgoing flux, and explicit time and integrability conventions.

rows.source_label: Contaminant mass conservation with flux f(q) = ubar q yields the advection equation
rows.next_foundation: Specialize the integral flux balance to the linear advection flux.

rows.source_label: Physical conservation of pressure and velocity is only approximate for very small disturbances in uniform media
rows.reason: This is the empirical small-disturbance modeling qualification. The separate ACOUSTICS-CONSERVATION-FORM row covers the exact algebraic assertion from the same paragraph.

rows.source_label: Sufficient smoothness of q and f(q) permits deriving (1.8) from the integral law (1.10)
rows.next_foundation: Formalize a fundamental-theorem-of-calculus bridge under explicit smoothness.

rows.source_label: Nonlinear conservation laws can develop discontinuities spontaneously from smooth initial data
rows.reason: The passage gives a broad possibility claim with no specified nonlinear flux, initial data, time interval, entropy solution, or shock criterion; formalizing it here would require inventing a theorem not stated in Chapter 1.

rows.source_label: At a discontinuity the differential equation fails classically while the integral conservation law continues to hold
rows.reason: The qualitative contrast depends on an unstated weak/entropy solution framework, trace convention, and class of discontinuities. Chapter 1 supplies none of the data needed for a nonvacuous universal theorem.

rows.source_label: A finite-volume unknown is the cell integral divided by cell volume rather than a point value
rows.next_foundation: Define one-dimensional cell averages on nondegenerate intervals.

rows.source_label: A time step modifies cell averages by edge fluxes computed from the available approximate averages
rows.next_foundation: Define a conservative one-step flux-difference update and prove telescoping conservation.

rows.source_label: Equation (1.11): Riemann initial data is q_l for x below zero and q_r for x above zero
rows.next_foundation: Define Riemann data while preserving the source's unspecified value at x = 0.

rows.source_label: Use neighboring cell averages as Riemann states to obtain numerical-flux and update information
rows.next_foundation: Define the interface-state adapter from adjacent cell averages.

rows.source_label: A hyperbolic Riemann solution is typically a function of x/t with finitely many constant-speed waves
rows.reason: The source explicitly qualifies this as typical and gives no theorem hypotheses, wave-count bound, admissibility condition, or nonlinear solution class.

rows.source_label: Solve linear hyperbolic Riemann data using eigenvalues and eigenvectors of A
rows.next_foundation: Search and audit an eigendata construction for linear hyperbolic Riemann data, preserving the unspecified value at the initial jump; construct missing foundations instead of skipping them.

rows.source_label: The simple wave structure extends to nonlinear systems with exact or arbitrarily accurate Riemann solutions constructible even for Euler
rows.reason: The broad exact-or-arbitrarily-accurate construction claim names no solver, error metric, admissibility class, hypotheses, or accuracy parameter and explicitly defers theory to later chapters.

rows.source_label: Shock or front tracking combines a smooth-region scheme with explicit discontinuity tracking and jump conditions
rows.reason: The paragraph only sketches a family of hybrid methods; it gives no front representation, smooth-region update, jump solver, time step, invariant, or correctness statement from which a checkable algorithm could be formalized.

rows.source_label: Shock capturing avoids explicit tracking, smears jumps over cells, and seeks correct jump conditions without nonphysical oscillations
rows.reason: The source describes a desired method class and qualitative behavior but specifies neither a numerical update nor definitions of smearing, correct jump conditions, or nonphysical oscillation.

rows.source_label: Use a normal Riemann solve at each two-dimensional edge or approximately planar three-dimensional face to determine flux
rows.reason: The chapter gives an implementation pattern without fixing a multidimensional mesh model, face orientation, normal-flux function, approximate Riemann solver, or update formula.

rows.source_label: On rectangular or logically rectangular grids, dimensional splitting solves one-dimensional coordinate-direction problems in turn
rows.next_foundation: Audit the existing ordered coordinate sweeps as function composition; preserve logically rectangular indexing and avoid attributing a fixed integrator or sweep order to Chapter 1.

rows.source_label: Assign heterogeneous material properties to each cell by averaging parameters over its volume
rows.next_foundation: Generalize the cell-average definition to material-parameter fields.

rows.source_label: Riemann data with jumps in both medium and state decomposes reflected and transmitted waves into neighboring cells
rows.reason: The reflected/transmitted-wave description omits the governing heterogeneous system, interface conditions, material parameter space, wave family, and solver, so Chapter 1 does not determine a theorem or executable construction.

rows.source_label: Wave-propagation methods use Riemann waves rather than interface fluxes, apply beyond conservation form, and connect to flux differencing on conservation laws
rows.reason: This is a high-level description of the wave-propagation framework. The fluctuation operators, interface update, applicability conditions, and claimed conservation-law correspondence are deferred and not specified in Chapter 1.

rows.source_label: q denotes the PDE solution while u is reserved for velocity or the x component of (u,v)
rows.reason: This is an editorial symbol convention, not a mathematical claim; Lean declarations already use typed identifiers that avoid the source's typographic ambiguity.

rows.source_label: For m equations q and Q are m-vectors and q^p denotes component p

rows.source_label: Superscripts enumerate eigenvalues lambda^p and eigenvectors r^p

rows.source_label: Initial data is denoted by a circle over the variable
